newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Split revealed in Khmer Rouge ranks.
newsitem.headline: Split revealed in Khmer Rouge ranks.

text.p: Khmer Rouge nominal leader Khieu Samphan on Wednesday accused a senior comrade of treason, revealing a split in the Maoist movement responsible for the 1970s "killing fields" reign of terror.
Khieu Samphan accused defence chief Son Sen and his wife of spying and seeking to destroy the Khmer Rouge's guerrilla army, called the army of Democratic Kampuchea (Cambodia).
"On June 9, 1997, the army of Democratic Kampuchea caught spies Son Sen, also known as Khieu, and (his wife) Yun Yat...," Khieu Samphan announced on clandestine Khmer Rouge radio.

He accused the couple of working on behalf of Cambodia's current co-Premier Hun Sen and neighbouring Vietnam to destroy the army and harm a political alliance recently formed by the country's other prime minister, Prince Norodom Ranariddh.
When asked about the report, Hun Sen said he had no knowledge of any spying within the Khmer Rouge.
But he told reporters he welcomed news of any breakdown within the Khmer Rouge that could end Cambodia's civil war.
"It is a good thing if we can find peace without using bullets," he said.

In an apparent softening of his previous opposition to amnesty for any of the rebel leaders, Hun Sen also said that if Khieu Samphan or Son Sen were to fight hated Khmer Rouge leader Pol Pot, he might consider discussing pardons.
The fate of Khieu Samphan, a consistent supporter of Ranariddh and his National United Front political alliance, has been just one area of difference between Hun Sen and Ranariddh.

The relationship between the two leaders, who formed an uneasy coalition after U.N.-sponsored elections in 1993, has grown increasingly bitter over power-sharing disputes and a keen competition to recruit Khmer Rouge rebels to their sides.
Khieu Samphan on Tuesday turned up the heat in the conflict by urging his rebels to fight Hun Sen, who fled to Vietnam after breaking with the Khmer Rouge in the mid-1970s.

Hun Sen returned in late 1978 with the Vietnamese invasion force that eventually overthrew the 1975-1979 Khmer Rouge rule in which more than one million Cambodians were killed. He later led the Hanoi-backed government that ruled until 1991.
The Khmer Rouge has waged a low-intensity war against the coalition government since reneging on the 1991 U.N.-sponsored peace pact that led to the 1993 elections.
But since last August, thousands of guerrillas have defected to the government and fewer than 2,000 fighters are thought to remain in the last rebel stronghold of Anlong Veng in the country's north.
